## 1. Problem Statement and Background

### Problem Definition

1.1 The central focus of this dataset is to provide insights into the factors influencing peoples' willingness to consider purchasing an electric vehicle (EV). In particular, this dataset includes factors ranging from peoples' age, income, and daily commute to their range anxiety level, environmental concern level, and whether or not a subsidy is available.   

1.2 The target audience may include any of the following:

* Automotive Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs): OEMs have a vested interest in consumer behavior and trends in
particular automotive subgroups. Electric vehicles are growing in popularity and charging stations are becoming more prevalent across the United States. This information may assist OEMs in determining the amount of resources they divert towards an electric fleet.

* Local City Governments: Public charging stations require investment and planning from government. This data and analysis may assist in determining to what degree charging stations should be prioritized for the benefit of their citizens. 

* Electric Utilities: Power companies would benefit from knowing how prevalent EVs are and how much they're influenced by local charging stations. If charging stations increased, there may be a change in peoples' willingness to buy EVs, and thus increase usage on these stations.  


1.3 Related Work: Prediction of Electic Vehicle (EV) sales is a big topic today. There are many approaches being used. In one study we found, researchers from National Pingtung University in Taiwan used Machine Learning to predict trends of EV sales on a macro scale. They talk about how machine learning has replaced more traditional linear regression or similar models. They also heavily considered the environmental impact of a large portion of the population switching to EVs. An article by Bloomberg addressed the trending topic of the proportion of EV ownership by country. These trends can tell manufacturers which countries to focus on. Many automotive manufacturers also run their own studies to help determine the viability of EV production. Most of these studies are focused on global or national trends. However, our project is focused on the prediction of whether individuals will purchase an EV or not. 

(Citations: https://www.sciencedirect.com/org/science/article/pii/S1062737523000574#secd5e912, https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/electric-vehicle-outlook/)


1.4 For measuring accuracy, since there is a large class imbalance (approximately 82.5% with 0 on Will_Buy_EV), a naive model assuming 0 for all data points would yield an 82.5% accuracy. So, accuracy will be a poor measure of success. Thus, measuring success will be done with the following:  

* AUC/ROC: Measuring a model's discriminatory power.

* Precision, Recall, and F1 Score: Ensuring the model minimizes false positives and false negatives.

* AIC/BIC: Comparing model performance across all four models used.

## 2. Data and Exploratory Analysis

2.1 The data set includes 15 features, including numerical, categorical, and character data types. The target feature is "Will_Buy_EV" which states whether an individual will express interest in buying an EV (0 for no, 1 for yes). The data is based on a real world situation but is synthetically-generated. 


Summary of Features: 

| Feature | Data Type |
| :----------------------: | :------------------: |
| **ID** | Integer |
| **Age** | Integer |
| **Annual Income USD** | Double |
| **Daily Commute (km)** | Double |
| **Number of Cars Owned** | Integer | 
| **Charging Stations Near Home** | Integer |
| **Charging Stations Near Work** | Integer |
| **Environmental Concern Level** | Double |
| **Gender** | Character |
| **City Type** | Character |
| **Current Car Type** | Character |
| **Home Charging Possible** | Character |
| **Subsidy Available** | Character |
| **Range Anxiety Level** | Character |
| **Will Buy EV** | Integer |

Looking at the structure of classes in the training dataset, 82.54% of individuals indicated no intent to purchase an EV, while 18.46% indicated an intent to purchase an EV.

2.2 Since this was a synthetically-generated dataset, there were no missing data points in any of the rows. The only transformation was to convert the target variable to a factor for plotting purposes. We found outliers for most of the numerical features, but given the large dataset, we decided not to remove any instances. 

2.3 The packages used so far are dplyr and tidymodels. dplyr is being used for the arrange() function to sort columns. tidymodels is used to generate training, validation, and test sets.

```{r Variable Selection, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
report <- data.frame(Independent_Variable = character(), 
                     Correlation = numeric())
options(scipen = 999)
for (var in variables) {
  if(is.numeric(train_data[[var]])){
    cors <- cor(train_data[[var]], as.numeric(train_data$Will_Buy_EV))
    #print(paste0("Correlation between ", var, " and target: ", round(cors, 5)))
    new_report <- data.frame(Independent_Variable = var,
                             Correlation = cors)
    report <- rbind(new_report, report)
  }
}

report <- report |>
  arrange(desc(abs(Correlation)))

report
```

* Figure 1 appears to show a positive correlation between environmental concern level and one's willingness to buy an EV. This feature appears to have the strongest linear correlation, so we anticipate it to be a more important feature in predicting willingness to buy an EV.

* Figure 2 shows the correlation between buying an EV dependent on age. There does not appear to be a strong correlation between the age of an individual and their willingness to buy an EV.

* Figure 3 shows the correlation between buying an EV dependent on annual income. There appears to be a positive linear relationship between income and willingness to buy an EV. As income increases, so does the willingness to buy an EV, on average.

* Figure 4 shows the correlation between buying an EV dependent on the number of charging stations near peoples house. This graph is surprising to us, as we expected the relationship to be strong and positive.

* Figure 5 shows the correlation between buying an EV dependent on the number of charging stations near work places. Similar to charging stations near home, there doesn't appear to be any relationship.

* Figure 6 shows the distribution of income present in the dataset. Incomes are generally normally distributed with some left skew due to incomes < $30K. From around 700,000 instances, the max annual income is around \$200,000 USD.

### EDA Conclusions:
Due to this being a synthetically generated data set, there are some weird behaviors with some of the features. Age appears to be uniformly distributed which does not match real world age distribution. We hypothesized that charging station availability would have a stronger correlation, but our initial graphs seem to show that almost no correlation exists with whether or not an individual will buy an EV. Based on our exploratory plots we think that Environmental Concern Level and Annual Income will be the best linear predictors for willingness to make an EV purchase.

## Methods   

1. Describe the methods you plan to use (models, data preparation, feature engineering)

* Baseline model: Given the high class imbalance (~82.5% individuals not expressing interest in purchasing an EV), a naive model would predict 0 for all individuals. So, it would have an accuracy of 82.5%.

* Logistic Regression - Our problem is a classification problem and logistic regression produces probabilities that certain individuals will be classified as expressing interest in buying an EV or not expressing that interest. Logistic regression only requires that the target variable be classified as a factor for predicting discrete values (0 or 1). 

* Random Forest - Also a classification algorithm. We have numerical and categorical features, so without needing to standardize our data, we can use both in the same model, effectively separating intervals of potential indicators for predicting willingness to buy an EV or not. No additional feature engineering, specifically standardization, is required.

* k-Means: Classification algorithm designed to produce clusters/centroids which attempt to categorize all data into distinct groups, each with a respective probability representing willingness to buy an EV or not. k-Means requires standardization since certain numerical features differ in scale. 

* e-Means: e-Means operates very similarly to k-Means but the primary difference is in the calculation of the clusters/centroids. Traditional k-Means operates on full-batch optimization, whereas e-Means resorts to mini-batch and handles updates through an exponential moving average.

* We decided against a single classification decision tree for this project and opted for random forest, since random forest utilizes many trees to aggregate their results and produce more consistent, average results. 


2. Justify your methods based on the problem. Mention methods you considered but did not use, and why

* Each of the algorithms we decided on are intended to solve classification problems. Since our target variable is a binary (0 or 1), we aim to correctly classify individuals as expressing interest in purchasing an EV or not. Any regression algorithms that produce a continuous value are unsuitable for the task, since a value between 0 and 1 is not interpretable. Linear regression, multiple linear regression, and any nonlinear regression would subsequently fail to produce an adequate prediction to the problem.

```{r calc_AUC function, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}

#helper function to compute ROC-AUC
#event_level = "second" to target "1" aka "yes" to Will_Buy_EV
calc_auc <- function(df, model_name) {
  auc <- roc_auc(df, truth = Will_Buy_EV, .pred_1, event_level = "second")$.estimate
  cat(sprintf("[%s] Validation ROC-AUC: %.4f\n", model_name, auc))
}

```


```{r Logistic Regression, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
#fit logistic regression with assumed valuable predictors
#predict Will_Buy_EV by features: everything except ID and also an interaction term of Income x ECL
#(whether or not being environmentally concerned has a stronger effect on wealthy citizens than non-wealthy citizens)
#underlying assumption is that ECL on its own is insufficient and some degree of income is required to make the decision to purchase an EV

logit_fit <- glm(Will_Buy_EV ~ . - id + Annual_Income_USD:Environmental_Concern_Level,
  data = train_data,family = binomial(link = "logit"))

# predict probabilities on validation data
val_preds_logit <- val_data |>
  mutate(.pred_1 = predict(logit_fit, newdata = val_data, type = "response"),
    .pred_0 = 1 - .pred_1)

calc_auc(val_preds_logit, "Logistic Regression")
# [Logistic Regression] Validation ROC-AUC: 0.9384
```


```{r Random Forest, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}

rf_fit <- ranger(formula = Will_Buy_EV ~ . - id,data = train_data,
  num.trees = 300, #bagging (bootstrap aggregating) - 300 independent decision trees
  probability = TRUE,       # outputs probabilities rather than hard 0 or 1 classes
  importance = "impurity",  # Gini feature importance rankings
  seed = 42)

# Predict on validation data
rf_pred_obj <- predict(rf_fit, data = val_data)

#mutate validation data for 2 columns: predicted prob that will_buy = 0 and 1
val_preds_rf <- val_data |>
  mutate(.pred_1 = rf_pred_obj$predictions[, "1"],
    .pred_0 = rf_pred_obj$predictions[, "0"])

calc_auc(val_preds_rf, "Random Forest")
#[Random Forest] Validation ROC-AUC: 0.9385
```

```{r k-means, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
# Select the continuous features identified during EDA
cluster_vars <- c("Annual_Income_USD", "Age", "Daily_Commute_km", "Environmental_Concern_Level")

#standardize using training set means and standard deviations (to avoid leakage from val data)
#k-means requires euclidean distance metric, so terms must be identical in axes
#income ranges between $20k : $200k, whereas ECL {1,2,3,4,5}
train_means <- sapply(train_data[cluster_vars], mean)
train_sds   <- sapply(train_data[cluster_vars], sd)

#converts train_scaled and val_scaled into N x 4 matrices, where N = # of rows
#4 columns - 1 for each of the cluster_vars converted to z-scores

train_scaled <- scale(train_data[cluster_vars], center = train_means, scale = train_sds)
val_scaled   <- scale(val_data[cluster_vars],   center = train_means, scale = train_sds)

# fit k-means on the scaled training data (k = 5 clusters), 10 different starting configs,
#and 25 number of reassignment iterations before stopping if centroids haven't converged
set.seed(42)
k_fit <- kmeans(train_scaled, centers = 5, nstart = 10, iter.max = 25)

k_rates <- train_data |>
  mutate(cluster = k_fit$cluster) |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarize(buy_rate = mean(Will_Buy_EV == "1"))


t(k_fit$centers) 

typeof(k_rates$buy_rate)

val_clusters_k <- apply(val_scaled, 1, function(individual) {
  #k-fit$centers is a 5x4 matrix: (5 clusters x 4 features)
  #transposing yields 4 x  matrix (4 features x 5 clusters)


  distances <- colSums((t(k_fit$centers) - individual)^2)
  #distances is now a vector full of values (distances) from each cluster
  #return index of min column (aka which cluster produced the minimal distance)
  #and assigns cluster # it most identifies the individual with
  which.min(distances)})

val_preds_kmeans <- val_data |>
  mutate(cluster=val_clusters_k,
         .pred_1 = k_rates$buy_rate[cluster],
         .pred_0 = 1 - .pred_1)

calc_auc(val_preds_kmeans, "k-Means Clustering")
#[k-Means Clustering] Validation ROC-AUC: 0.7779
```


```{r e-means, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}

set.seed(42)
emeans_fit <- emeans(train_scaled, k=5)

print(emeans_fit$centers)

emeans_rates <- train_data |>
  mutate(cluster = emeans_fit$cluster) |>
  group_by(cluster) |>
  summarize(total = n(),
            buyers = sum(Will_Buy_EV == "1"),
            buy_rate = mean(Will_Buy_EV == "1")) |>
  arrange(cluster)

print(emeans_rates |> arrange(desc(buy_rate)))

val_clusters_e <- apply(val_scaled, 1, function(person) {
  distances <- colSums((t(emeans_fit$centers) - person)^2)
  which.min(distances)})

val_preds_emeans <- val_data |>
  mutate(cluster = val_clusters_e,
         .pred_1 = emeans_rates$buy_rate[cluster],
         .pred_0 = 1 - .pred_1)

calc_auc(val_preds_emeans, "e-Means Clustering")
#[e-Means Clustering] Validation ROC-AUC: 0.7884
```


```{r Result Comparison, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
roc_all <- bind_rows(
  val_preds_logit  |> mutate(model = "Logistic Regression"),
  val_preds_rf     |> mutate(model = "Random Forest"),
  val_preds_kmeans |> mutate(model = "k-Means (k=5)"),
  val_preds_emeans |> mutate(model = "e-means (k=5)")) |>
  group_by(model) |>
  roc_curve(truth = Will_Buy_EV, .pred_1, event_level = "second")

autoplot(roc_all) +
  labs(
    title = "ROC Curves",
    x = "False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)",
    y = "True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)"
  )
```
